w4 'candi sugar gives an aromatic reminiscent of burnt sugar and raisins' supports raisin/burnt sugar; the 'fig and dried fruits' element rests only on w3, a forum-hosted product blurb about one product ('Dark 2 (D2) Belgian Candi Syrup').

w12 'Special B for raisin flavors' and w13 'raisin-like flavour' (Castle spec page) support the core. The 'used sparingly ... toasted raisin, figs, cherry, or plum' part (w15) says only 'from it'; the quote never names Special B. Two organisations (bjcp, castlemalting) support the core, so the güçlü label holds.
w12 'CaraMunich for dried fruit flavors'.

Each element is in its quotes (w8 'esters ... go up with increasing temperature', w10 'ferment cool you will suppress more of the esters', w9 '68-70° F ... fruity yeast-derived notes'). But the item offers 'raise temperature' as a way to get raisin/dark fruit, while w7 in the same list says 'At lower temperatures, Abbaye produces darker...' fruit. It also leaves out that w8 says phenols and higher alcohols rise too, and the 'cool suppresses more' element comes from a forum post.
w6 on the WLP530 page (w5) says 'Produces cherry, plum and pear esters'. The drop was a false alarm: product matching read 'pear' as the ingredient Armut.

Both elements are verbatim in the quotes (w5 'prime variable ... is fermentation temperature', w6 'esters, phenols, and higher alcohol production go up'). Framing 'raise temperature' as the top lever for raisin/plum conflicts with w7 in this question: 'At lower temperatures, Abbaye produces darker fruit aromas and flavors of raisin, date and fig'.
w10 '68-70° F (20-21° C) range will help develop fruity yeast-derived notes without the fusel alcohol character' is translated faithfully.
w17 'Dark caramelized sugar syrup or sugars for color and rum-raisin flavors'.

w7 'At lower temperatures, Abbaye produces darker fruit aromas and flavors of raisin, date and fig'. False alarm on the ingredient Hurma (date). This dropped item was the counter-evidence to the shown 'raise temperature' item.

w12 'darker crystal malts (80–150°L) add a dark fruit, raisin-plum note' and w13 'raisin-like flavour'. The 80/150 numbers belong to the crystal malts, not to Château Special Belgium, so the 'wrong value' drop is a false alarm.

w3 'which increased the protein’s flexibility, leading to enhanced foaming, stability, and texture of the foam' supports the effect. But the antecedent of 'which' (the PZ–iso-α-acid interaction in w2) is inferred across truncated snippets, and this is a lab binding study presented as a general foam effect.
w1 'Tetra is the common choice for improving beer foam stabilit...'.

w4 'Protein in the proper form and amounts ... promotes head retention' supports the protein part. The 'high-protein malts' part rests on the truncated w5 heading 'Choose the Right Malt / Malts high in prote...'.
w7 'Extracts lose much of the foam-building proteins during processing'.
w8 'low in protein such as corn, rice, and sugar adjuncts tend to dilute foam-positive compounds'.
w1 'Dextrins give beer fuller body and aid in head retention'. It does not endorse the user's lactose premise.

w3 'The high carbonation level gives a very thick, rocky, mousse-like white head that is very long-lasting' is a description of German Weissbier. The item states it for any beer without that style context (the user's recipe is a Weizen, which softens this).

w2 'Lactose ... may be used to increase body and mouthfeel' and w4 'Lactose adds fullness, body, and mou...'. 'The quotes do not mention foam' is also true. The drop was a false alarm, and this was the item that answered the user's lactose question directly.
w1 'prevents chill haze' and w2 'For use at the beginning of fermentation' (manufacturer claim). Note: the Brulosophy test (w3, shown as C14#1) found more haze, but it is not this item's own source.
w3 'it maintained more haze than the batch that wasn’t fined with Clarity Ferm' is faithful. It drops the nuance 'slightly clearer than before'.
w4 'rapidly decreasing the temperature ... encourages the coagulation of particulates such as proteins and yeast' and w5 'The cold crashed version was definitely less opaque'.
w6 'samples at 3 weeks ... at least to my eyes, they looked the sam[e]'. 'Gözle' keeps the hedge.

w10 'primary cause of haze is from proteins and polyphenols ... from malts and hops', w9 'Chill haze ... comprised of proteins and polyphenols', and w11 'reduce the amount of haze-forming proteins, reduce the amount of polyphenols'.

w1 'dry-hopped versions may be slightly hazy' and w3 'dry hopped beers tend to be a bit cloudy, since some of the polyphenols were extracted post-boil'. Two organisations support it (labelled olası, so this is under-rated rather than an error).
w9 'the beer dry hopped at yeast was notably more clear than the standard dry hop batch' (single experiment, labelled olası).
w5 'Isinglass ... binds to negatively charged yeast cells aiding in yeast precipitation' and w6 'Protofine ... promoting yeast and protein flocculation to improve ... beer haze'.
w7 (SafAle S-04 page) 'Due to its flocculation power, tends to produce beers with higher clarity'.

w11 'Both dry hopped then cold crashed and fined their beers with gelatin' supports the practice. The '36 °F (2 °C)' number comes from one recipe's instructions (w13 'cold crash to 36 °F') but is merged into the plural 'ödüllü tariflerde'.
w2 'gelatin will result in slower clarification than will the higher MW isinglass'; w5 'collagen from gelatin is not as effective a fining as isinglass' - both elements present.

Dose matches w3 '1/2-1 teaspoon (4-8 g) ... per 5 gallons (19 L)'. But w4 'It may, however, take 2-3 weeks before the beer becomes properly clear' is a separate snippet; 'however' signals a contrast, and the quote does not show that the 2-3 weeks applies to this gelatin dose. Pairing them as factor -> effect is unsupported.
w9 'In addition to removing yeast, Gelatin also helps settle these polyphenols out of the beer.'
w12 'crash to 35°F (2°C) and add gelatin finings. (For best results, wait 24 hours and add a second round of gelatin.)' - framed as recipe instruction.

w7 'Chill haze is formed when proteins and polyphenols/tannins react at cool temperatures'; w8 'prevented by adding silica gels or PVPP to adsorb chill haze reactants'. Drop reason (Tanen product) was a false alarm.

w8 'raise the temperature into the 65 to 68 °F (18 to 20 °C) range for a two-day period near the end'; w6 'reduce the diacetyl precursor alpha-acetolactate, which the yeast create during the early phase'.
w7 'diacetyl reduction is slower at colder temperatures, a cold-fermented lager may require a diacetyl rest'; w14 'lager yeast ferments and reabsorbs diacetyl at a slower rate due to temperature'.
w15 'less prevalent in ales which get fermented at a higher temperature'.
w16 'as alpha-acetolactate is oxidized and turns into 2,3 butanedione (diacetyl)'.

w4 BSI-950 'low diacetyl production'; w1/w2 White Labs strain 'low diacetyl' + 'benefits from a diacetyl rest and conditioning'; w3 Wyeast Bavarian Lager 'thorough diacetyl rest is recommended'. Caveat: the names 'WLP838' and '2206' appear only through the URLs (whitelabs id=226, wyeast bavarian-lager), not in the quote text. There is no taste judgement, so the drop was a false alarm.

w2 'Ales do well with a 2- to 4-day diacetyl rest at 70° F following fermentation.' Note: w1 says temperature modification is not necessary for ales, so the two are in mild tension, but the item makes no recommendation.
w1 'fermentation temperature is usually 65 to 70 °F (18 to 21 °C), so temperature modification is not necessary'. The quote is truncated at 'But the fermentat...', so a caveat may follow.

Core claim matches w7 'Due to this strain's high flocculation - Slight diacetyl production is common.' But the strain name 'WLP002' is not in the quote (only the URL id=102), and the factor heading generalises to 'yüksek flokülasyonlu maya suşu'.

w8 'Eliminate the risk of diacetyl formation ... Adding Brewzyme D with your yeast pitch results in the decarboxylation of alpha...'; w12 'Chico yeast without ALDC ... typical diacetyl profile ... increasing'. Brewzyme D = ALDC is not stated, 'alpha-acetolactate' is completed from truncated text, and a manufacturer marketing claim ('eliminate the risk') is stated as fact.

w4 'WLP001 is also quick at reabsorbing diacetyl' (directly contradicts the drop reason); w6 '...is a good diacetyl reducer' on the same BYO page as w5 'Wyeast 1056'. The subject of w6 is truncated but plausibly 1056.

w10 'If the boil time decreases, straw-colored beers brewed with Pilsner malts start to show DMS'; w9 '90 minutes, which helps reduce the S-Methyl Methionine (SMM) present in the lightly kilned Pilsner malt'. Note: w4/w5/w2 in the same question (25-min boil, no DMS) conflict with this, and the card does not flag the conflict.

Taster part is OK: w5 'not a single person identified a DMS off-flavor' (2020 single Pils, 25 min). But the lab part comes from w2, a different BYO-cited 'latter exBEERiment': 'neither beer contained measurabl...' refers to two beers. Neither quote makes the merged claim that the 25-min Pils was lab-tested with two beers showing no DMS, and 'DMS' is also completed from truncated text.
w8 'Rapid wort cooling also limits ... DMS that can continue to be formed from the conver...'. 'SMM' is supplied by inference from the truncated text and is not in the quote.
w7 'heat-sensitive and is lost to a great extent during malt kilning' (subject 'It' = SMM per uncited w6 on the same page); w12 'As malt color increases, SMM and DMS levels reduce.'
w3 'it's possible the lack of DMS in these beers is a function of the high modification of the Pils malt used'. The hedge is preserved ('olası nedeni').

w3 'steam will condense on the surfaces of the kettle and drip back into the wort, resulting in a higher concentration...'. 'DMS' is completed from truncated text, and this is the experiment's stated premise, presented as an established effect even though the same experiment (w4) found no perceptible difference.

w4 'My inability to reliably distinguish ... suggests any differences in DMS ...'. The conclusion is truncated, so 'algılanamadığı' is inferred, and 'my' (a single taster, the author) is dropped in favour of the impersonal 'ayırt edilemedi'.

w8 'Pilsner malt contains as much as eight times the SMM of pale malt or other malts kilned at moderate to high temperatures'; w7 'lightly kilned malts hold on to as much as eight times'. Two organisations support it (app counted 1).
w11 'DMS and DMSO are volatile and will evaporate if you have a strong rolling boil'; w12 'increasing the power input of a burner ... significantly reduced the levels of measured DMS'.

w10 'Since Pilsner malt is the majority of the grist, plan on using at least a 90-minute boil to ensure enough of the malt derived SMM...'. No taste judgement, so the drop was a false alarm. Brulosophy w2 conflicts, but the content matches its source.

w2 'To my palate, the 1:1 sulfate-to-chloride beer had a much rounder bitterness'. The perception is correctly attributed to the experimenter, not stated as the app's own judgement.

w6 forum 'It does not give you a more intense bitterness in my experience.' The quote is faithful but the factor is undefined (the item itself admits the subject is unclear). Support is a single forum anecdote, mis-tagged as [dergi].
w10 'a drier beer needs less bitterness to seem balanced'; w9 'finish should not have much residual sugar' (supports the parenthetical).

w13 'medium to low cohumulone ... smoother bittering profile in my opinion'; w15 'bitterness was smooth and didn't linger ... due to Simcoe's low cohumulone'; w12 'popular view ... high in cohumulone are "harsh"'. The opinion framing is preserved.

w3 'sulfate-to-chloride ratio of 2:1 or higher will tend to give the beer a drier, more assertive hop balance'; w1 'reliably distinguish an American Pale Ale with a 3:1 sulfate-to...' (single-taster, semi-blind). The drop reason ('2 (Pale Ale Malt)') misread the ratio as a product value, so it was a false alarm.

w4 'higher amounts of sulfate produce a more pronounced bitterness'; w3 'more assertive bitterness with a hop character that popped out'; w5 'ratio of 2:1 or higher ... drier, more assertive hop balance'. All elements present; w3 is the author's personal impression but w4/w5 carry it.
w6 '"permanent hardness" does accentuate and sharpen hop bitterness' - faithful.

w7 'temporary hardness tends to make for a harsher bitter flavor'; w9 'high pH, high residual alkalinity ... can lead to harshness in a pale hoppy beer'; w10 'carbonates ... interfere with the perception of bitterness'. (w9 also lists high sulfate; omitted, not contradicted by the item.)

w1 'unique sample was selected 8 times (p=0.003) ... reliably distinguish an American Pale Ale with a 3:1 sulfate-to...' + w2 '1:1 sulfate-to-chloride beer had a much rounder bitterness'; post-fermentation CaCl2 in w1/w2 URL. Drop was a false alarm (single semi-blind taster though).

w11 'tasters ... unable to reliably distinguish an American Pale Ale that received a post-fermentation gyp[sum]'; w12 'difference in sulfate levels ... was 154 ppm'. Value 154 is ppm sulfate, not tied to Pale Ale Malt - false alarm.
w5 'The solubility of CO2 increases as the temperature decreases'; w3 'the lower the temperature ... the more CO2 gas will stay in solution'.
w5 'solubility of CO2 also increases with increasing gas pressure'; w3 'the higher the pressure, the more CO2 gas will stay in solution'.
w4 'For a given amount of priming sugar, the greater the headspace, the lower the carbonation' - exact.

Content matches w7 'psi alone is meaningless to carbonation without taking into consideration the beer temp', but the only support is a forum post (forum.homebrewersassociation.org, mis-tagged [dergi]).

Subtraction part OK (w8 'Subtracting 0.85 from 2.4 gives you 1.55 volumes'). But '3/4 bardak mısır şekeri yaklaşık 2.5 hacim CO2 üretir' merges w9 (truncated before any volume number: 'would yie...') with w10 ('This will produce about 2.5 volumes' - antecedent not in quote); neither quote states the combined claim, and the batch volume (w9 context) is dropped, making the dose figure unanchored.
w8 'dependent on three factors: the carbonation level desired ..., the CO_2 content of the beer at bottling, and the amount...' - faithful, truncation acknowledged.

Kräusening definition supported by w13 'carbonating a finished batch of beer with actively fermenting wort'; speise as unfermented wort by w15. The Schneider Weissbier claim rests only on w14, a reader comment ('Dave Hartley September 30, 2019 ... Schneider Weissebier is carbonated by ... adding Speise') - anecdote.

w4 'Aim for 3 to 3.5 volumes (6 to 7 g/L) ... can cause many normal beer bottles to explode' and w16 'Schneider targets 3.5 volumes of CO2 in the bottle' OK. 'Buğday biralarında 3-4 hacim' cites w2 'These beers have CO2 levels ranging from three to four volumes' - the antecedent (wheat and fruit beers) is only in uncited w1. Also card does not flag w6's 2.5 volumes as conflicting.

w6 'package and carbonate to a healthy 2.5 volumes of CO2' from the make-your-best-weissbier article; item correctly hedges as 'bir kaynakta'. (Conflicts with C25#2 sources; not flagged as a contradiction on the card.)
w7 'bottling beer that contains little or no carbon dioxide and then adding priming sugars that yeast will ferm[ent]' supports it; no '2' value appears in the item - false alarm.

w4 'Keeping the fermentation temperature in the 68-70° F (20-21° C) range will help develop fruity yeast-derived notes without the fusel alcohol character' - exact (Dubbel recipe; user's beer is a Dubbel).
w14 'Controlling temperature is important to getting a proper level of attenuation and avoiding off-flavors, especially if you are making a bigger beer' - exact.
w9 'if you don't pitch enough, you get solventy' - faithful.
w5 'Initially adding oxygen reduces the amount of esters ..., but high levels of oxygen also increase the amount of fusel alcohols' - faithful.

Item text tracks w1 'fermenter height plays a role in flavor development, with very tall fermenters ... suppressing e...', but it is presented as a factor of hot/fusel alcohol while the quote says nothing about alcohol (suppressed object is truncated, likely esters); 'flavor' rendered as 'aroma'.
w2 'esters, phenols, and higher alcohol production go up with increasing temperature' - exact.
w3 '68-70° F (20-21° C) range will help develop fruity yeast-derived notes without the fusel alcohol character' - exact.

w5 'Ferment at 64°F (18°C) to start and increase slowly almost immediately'; w6 'The goal is to minimize warm alcohols but also to promote complete fermentation and some yeast flavor contributions' (same article).

w8 'With increasing numbers of cells introduced into the wort, the content of the esters and fusel alcohols increased, while the acetaldehyde concentratio[n]...' - faithful. But the same paper (jib.242, w9) is shown in C27#4 with the opposite direction for higher alcohols; the card lists both without flagging the contradiction.

w9 'extension of yeast dosage of 10–50 million CFU in mL ... caused a marked reduction in the concentration of higher alcohols. However, fu...' - core supported, but the 'However, fu[sel]...' qualifier is dropped, 'yüksek alkol' is ambiguous (reads as high ABV, not higher alcohols), and the same paper (w8, C27#3) says fusel alcohols increased with more cells - presented as an action without stating the conflict.

w6 'Higher temperature and dissolved oxygen ... decreased tropical, citrus, and hoppy ... expression of malty' supports effect; w5 says DO had 'a lesser, but significant, impact' but the comparator (temperature) is not in the snippet, it is inferred.
w4 'dominant oxidized characters in pale, light-tasting beers is a papery or cardboard-like flavor caused by ... aldehydes'.
w11 'main mechanism contributing to the generation of trans-2-nonenal ... enzymatic or nonenzymatic oxidation of lipids'. Note: contradicts C28#3 (w10) and the card does not flag the conflict.

w9 'no significant difference in trans-2-nonenal ... oxygen-receiving and oxygen-free beers after aging' supports; w10 'not due to lipid oxidation in the...' has a truncated scope qualifier that the Turkish drops, stating it unconditionally.
w3 'one study found it unimportant in top-fermented ales, especially darker ones'.
w1 'Astringency is a physical mouthfeel caused by the association and precipitation of large polyphenols with proline-rich proteins in the saliva'.
w2 'addition of polyphenols to beer induced harsh bitterness and increased astringency'.
w3 'tannins contribute to astringent' supports it; drop was a false product match (Tannin powder).
w4 'extraction of tannins from grain husks due to overcrushing, oversparging, or sparging with water having a pH over 6.0'; w5 'sparge water pH to remain under 6.0, which may require acidification'.
w6 'Less contact time with heat extracts less tannins, which makes for a smoother beer'.
w8 'Lagering reduces sulfur compounds and other fermentation byproducts'; w15 'sulfur odors tend to fade with time and aging'.
w15 'sulfur is scrubbed out by CO2 during active fermentation'; w9 'venting out the CO2, I was also venting out the hydrogen sulfide'.

w3 'cooler, slower fermentations result in less CO2 scrubbing' supports, but the Turkish 'Daha az CO2 ile surüklenme saglar' reads as 'provides scrubbing with less CO2', which can invert the meaning (less sulfur removal).

w12 'Low nitrogen levels will limit the rate of this reaction, leaving excess hydrogen sulfide'; w4 'poor wort nutrition ... elevated levels of H2S and ... rotten eggs'. 2 orgs (beerandbrewing.com, lallemandbrewing.com) -> strong ok.
w16 'To reduce sulfur production ... pitch enough yeast ... lagers often require twice as much yeast as a typical ale'.
w1 'it takes 7 to 9 days to fully utilize aroma'; w2 'just a few days can lead to an unpleasant raw hop flavor'. Note: conflicts with C31#1 (limit to a week or less); card does not flag it.
w3 'Limit contact time of dry hops ... to a week or less to help limit the vegetal flavors'. Own source consistent; cross-item tension with C31#0 (7-9 days).

w4 'initial stages of fermentation large quantities of CO2 ... will scrub ...' (object truncated, 'aroma' inferred); w5 'only ... when the primary fermentation has subsided (after three or four days)' supports timing.

w6 'Whirlpool additions produced beers with the highest concentrations of geraniol, linalool, and beta-citronellol'; w7 'despite the popularity of dry hopping ... whirlpool additions can produce more intensely aromatic bee[rs]' - hedged 'üretebilir' kept.

Merges two separate facts: w8 (Brulosophy) '60C whirlpool ... 12.5% more linalool than a 90C' with w9 (HBA bitterness article) 'Despite the 30° F difference ... sensory evaluation was highly inconclusive'. 60C vs 90C is a 30 C (54 F) difference; neither quote says the 60/90C comparison was sensorially inconclusive.
